extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, copyeditors, and publishers preparing/managing scholarly and book-length prose
extracted.subtask_description: Practical style rules for spelling, punctuation, and related typographic conventions for scholarly and book publishing (University of Chicago Manual of Style excerpt). Covers word-formation, use of -ise/-ize, and detailed rules for periods, commas, colons, semicolons, dashes, parentheses, brackets, ellipses, hyphens, apostrophes, and quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed compounds for certain pronouns and time words
rubrics_metrics.description: Make one word of 'anyone,' 'someone,' 'everyone,' 'today,' 'tomorrow,' 'tonight,' 'cannot' (see 204). Distinguish between 'sometimes' and 'some time(s).'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer closed forms for listed words; be attentive to sense distinction between adverb 'sometimes' and phrase 'some time(s)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate -ise and -ize terminations
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate between the terminations -ise and -ize as follows: lists of words that should be spelled with -ise vs those with -ize (-yze).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the provided lists: e.g., advertise, comprise, supervise, etc., with -ise; aggrandize, analyze, authorize, etc., with -ize. Use the lists as prescriptive guidance for standard spelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation font/style matching
rubrics_metrics.description: All punctuation marks should be printed in the same style or font of type as the word or letter immediately preceding them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure punctuation adopts roman/italic/cap style consistent with preceding word (examples shown).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of period to end complete sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: A period is used to indicate the end of a complete sentence. (See 125.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply periods for sentence termination; consult other numbered rules for exceptions and placement relative to abbreviations and headings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periods after abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a period after all abbreviations, except where a mechanical necessity compels the omission of letters in the middle of a word for which there is no recognized abbreviated form; omission may be indicated by an apostrophe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat metric symbols as abbreviations (period), but not chemical symbols, 'per cent,' or book-format abbreviations; follow journal-specific exceptions noted (e.g., Astrophysical Journal).

rubrics_metrics.name: No period after certain recognized abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use a period, in technical matter, after the recognized abbreviations for linguistic epochs or after initials-only titles of well-known publications, nor after 'MS' (= manuscript).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: IE, OE, MHG, AJSL, ZAW, CIL, MS — omit final period.

rubrics_metrics.name: No period after Roman numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use no period after Roman numerals, even if having the value of ordinals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vol. IV; Louis XVI was on the throne.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit period after running-heads and certain headings
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the period after running-heads; after centered headlines; after side-heads set in separate lines; after cut-in heads; after box-heads in tables; and after superscriptions and legends that do not form a complete sentence, and after date lines at top of communications, and after signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult rule 50 and 279-283 for definitions; applies to non-sentential headings and similar elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periods inside quotation marks and parentheses rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The period is placed inside the quotation marks; and inside the parentheses when the matter enclosed is an independent sentence and forms no part of the preceding sentence; otherwise outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a rule without exception for periods inside quotation marks. Place parentheses-period inside only for independent enclosed sentences; otherwise put period outside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of exclamation point
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclamation point is used to mark an outcry, or an emphatic or ironical utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place exclamation point inside the quotation marks when part of the quotation; otherwise outside (see examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of interrogation point (question mark)
rubrics_metrics.description: The interrogation point is used to mark a query, or to express a doubt. Indirect questions should not be followed by an interrogation point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the interrogation point inside quotation marks only when it is part of the quotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon usage — general
rubrics_metrics.description: The colon is used to 'mark a discontinuity of grammatical construction greater than that indicated by the semicolon and less than that indicated by the period.' Common uses: (i) emphasize a close connection between two complete clauses; (2) separate a clause which is grammatically complete from a second which contains an illustration or amplification; (3) to introduce a formal statement, extract, speech, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a connecting conjunction like 'that' immediately connects the clauses, do not use a colon. Use comma before quotation of a clause mid-sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon as replacement for 'namely' or 'as follows'
rubrics_metrics.description: The colon often takes the place of an implied 'namely,' 'as follows,' 'for instance,' or similar phrase. Where such a word/phrase is used and followed by one or more grammatically complete clauses, follow with a colon; otherwise with a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use colon when what follows are complete clauses; use comma for non-clausal follow-ups (see examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon after salutatory phrases and addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a colon after the salutatory phrase at the beginning of a letter, and after the introductory remark of a speaker addressing the chairman or audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'MY DEAR MR. BROWN:'; 'Mr. Chairman, Ladies and Gentlemen:'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon between chapter and verse and hours and minutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a colon between chapter and verse in Scripture passages, and between hours and minutes in time indications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Matt. 2:5-13; 4:30 P.M.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon between place of publication and publisher
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a colon between the place of publication and the publisher's name in literary and bibliographical references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Clement of Alexandria (London: Macmillan), II, 97.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon placement relative to quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The colon should be placed outside the quotation marks, unless it is part of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place colon outside unless quote itself includes the colon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon general function
rubrics_metrics.description: A semicolon is used to mark the division of a sentence somewhat more independent than that marked by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use semicolons where clauses are more independent; example sentences illustrate rhythm and linkage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon in complex enumerations
rubrics_metrics.description: In enumerations use a semicolon between the different links if these consist of more than a few words closely connected, especially if individual clauses contain internal punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use semicolons to separate long or punctuated items in a series; see examples with parenthetical remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon in Scripture references
rubrics_metrics.description: In Scripture references a semicolon is used to separate passages containing chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon placement relative to quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The semicolon should be placed outside the quotation marks, unless it is part of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat semicolon like colon and comma rules for quotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma general definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma is 'used to indicate the smallest interruptions in continuity of thought or grammatical construction, the marking of which contributes to clearness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to mark small breaks, appositives, lists, and for clarity; many illustrative examples provided to show subtle distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma separating proper nouns of different individuals/places
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate proper nouns belonging to different individuals or places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'To John, Smith was always kind'; 'To America, Europe awards the prize...' Ensures clarity between possessive/associative names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before final 'and/or/nor' in a series (Oxford comma)
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma before 'and,' 'or,' and 'nor' connecting the last two links in a sequence of three or more; always put a comma before 'etc.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Oxford comma for clarity; but omit when links are brief and closely knit. Examples contrast both usages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma with clauses introduced by conjunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily, put a comma before and after clauses introduced by conjunctions such as 'and,' 'but,' 'if,' 'while,' 'as,' 'whereas,' 'since,' etc., especially if a change of subject takes place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use comma when the preceding clause is not complete without them, or in brief close-welded phrases; many examples illustrate correct/incorrect use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma around introductory adverbs/phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Adverbs and phrases like 'now,' 'then,' 'however,' 'indeed,' 'therefore,' 'moreover,' etc., should be followed by a comma when standing at the beginning of a sentence or clause, and set off by commas when inserted in the middle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use a comma when connection is logically close or structural smooth; exceptions include 'therefore' after a verb, 'indeed' with adjectives/adverbs it qualifies, or adverbs like 'perhaps' and 'also' usually uncommaed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma omission before 'rather' in certain expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: A comma is preferably omitted before 'rather' in expressions like '...measured in this way rather than by ...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use judgment when phrase is tightly bound; rule illustrated with example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma with multiple adjectives preceding noun
rubrics_metrics.description: If among several adjectives preceding a noun the last bears a more direct relation to the noun than the others, it should not be preceded by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'the admirable political institutions of the country' vs 'a handsome, wealthy young man.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma with participial clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Participial clauses, especially those that contain an explanation of the main clause, should usually be set off by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Being asleep, he did not hear him.' Use to mark explanatory participial phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before 'not' introducing antithetical clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma before 'not' introducing an antithetical clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Men addict themselves to inferior pleasures, not because they deliberately prefer them...' Use comma to signal contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas vs dashes for parenthetical content
rubrics_metrics.description: For parenthetical, adverbial, or appositional clauses or phrases use commas to indicate structurally disconnected but logically integral interpolations; use dashes to indicate both structurally and logically disconnected insertions; never use the two together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose punctuation based on degree of disruption; examples demonstrate usage and caution against combining comma + dash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma between identical or closely similar words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate two identical or closely similar words, even if the sense or grammatical construction does not require it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Whatever is, is good'; 'What he was, is not known.' Use for rhetorical clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas around complementary/qualifying adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: In adjectival phrases, a complementary, qualifying, delimiting, or antithetical adjective added to the main epithet preceding a noun should be preceded and followed by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'This harsh, though perfectly logical, conclusion.' Use commas to bracket the qualifying adjective phrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas separating coordinated clauses modifying another clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more coordinate clauses ending in a word governing or modifying another word in a following clause should be separated by commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example constructions provided; use commas to mark such coordinate constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas to separate two numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate two numbers (date/page contexts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'In 1905, 347 teachers attended the convention'; November 1, 1905.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma for omission of repeated words
rubrics_metrics.description: A comma is employed to indicate the omission, for brevity or convenience, of a word or words the repetition of which is not essential to the meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use in constructions like 'In Illinois there are seventeen such institutions; in Ohio, twenty-two; in Indiana, thirteen.' Avoid when repetition is smooth enough not to require commas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before brief direct quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: A direct quotation, maxim, or similar expression, when brief, should be separated from the preceding part of the sentence by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'God said, Let there be light.' Use comma before short quoted passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before 'of' with residence/position
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma before 'of' in connection with residence or position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Mr. and Mrs. McIntyre, of Detroit, Mich.' Exceptions when place-name is effectively part of a title (e.g., Clement of Alexandria).

rubrics_metrics.name: No comma between consecutive pages in references (use en-dash)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use a comma between consecutive pages in literary references; use the en-dash; exceptions may be made for scriptural references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: pp. 4, 7-8, 10; use en-dash for ranges; some journals differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma after digits indicating thousands (except dates/page refs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma after digits indicating thousands, except when used as a date or in a page-reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 1,276; 10,419; January, 1909 (date is an exception for thousands rule depending on style). Note journal exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma separating month and year
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate month and year, and similar time divisions, by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: November, 1905; New Year's Day, 1906. Note some journals omit this comma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit commas in signatures and certain opening lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the comma, in signatures and at the beginning of articles, after author's name followed by address, title, or position in a separate line, or after address followed by a date line, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show layout of name and titles without commas (JAMES P. ROBINSON, address lines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma placement always inside quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma is always placed inside the quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow American usage: commas inside closing quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostrophe for contractions and omitted figures
rubrics_metrics.description: An apostrophe is used to mark the omission of a letter or letters in the contraction of a word, or of figures in a number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ne'er, don't, 'twas; class of '96; m'f'g for manufacturing; consult rule 123 for related abbreviation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming the possessive with apostrophe
rubrics_metrics.description: The possessive case of nouns, common and proper, is formed by the addition of an apostrophe, or apostrophe and s (see 113).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a man's, horses' tails; Scott's Ivanhoe, Jones's farms; special case forms like Themistocles' era.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural of numerals and rare coinages with apostrophe
rubrics_metrics.description: The plural of numerals, and of rare or artificial noun-coinages, is formed by the aid of an apostrophe and s; of proper nouns of more than one syllable ending in a sibilant, by adding an apostrophe alone (monosyllabic proper names ending in a sibilant add es; others, s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in the 1900's; in two's and three's; the Y.M.C.A.'s; use apostrophe+s with numerals and coinages, follow special rules for proper names ending in sibilants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks rules (referenced)
rubrics_metrics.description: See sections on 'Quotations' (74-91) for detailed rules on quotation marks use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotation-mark guidance is cross-referenced; pairing with comma/period/colon/semicolon placement discussed in related rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash usage general
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash is used to denote 'a sudden break, stop, or transition in a sentence, or an abrupt change in its construction, a long or significant pause, or an unexpected or epigrammatic turn of sentiment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dashes for strong interruptions, abrupt shifts, or emphatic apposition; many illustrative examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dashes for parenthetical clauses that are both logically and structurally independent
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dashes (rarely parentheses) for parenthetical clauses which are both logically and structurally independent interpolations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples demonstrate when dashes give clearer separation than commas or parentheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash to introduce emphasis or expansion repeating a word/phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: A clause added to lend emphasis to, or to explain or expand, a word or phrase occurring in the main clause, which word or phrase is then repeated, should be introduced by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '...important — the history of events and ideas.' Use dash before emphatic repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dash where 'namely' is implied
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a 'namely' is implied before a parenthetical or complementary clause, a dash should preferably be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'These discoveries — gunpowder, printing-press, compass, and telescope — were...' Use dash to signal enumeration following 'namely'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash before final-summarizing clause in broken-up sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: In sentences broken up into clauses, the final-summarizing clause should be preceded by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example with list-of-items followed by summarizing clause; dash signals summation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash after a line-heading followed by paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: A word or phrase set in a separate line and succeeded by paragraphs, at the beginning of each of which it is implied, should be followed by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use in enumerative or directive lists (e.g., 'I recommend — 1. That we kill him. 2. That we flay him.').

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash with side-heads
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash should be used in connection with side-heads, whether 'run in' or paragraphed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dash to separate side-heads from following text; examples given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of en-dash vs em-dash and number/date ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: Use en-dash in place of the word 'to' connecting two words or numbers (May–July, 1906); use em-dash for sentence breaks (May 1, 1905 — November 1, 1906). In connecting consecutive numbers, omit hundreds from the second number unless the first ends in two ciphers; in citing dates B.C. repeat hundreds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow numeric contraction rules for ranges; note journal exceptions that may require repeating hundreds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash preceding reference after direct quotation in footnotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a dash precede the reference (author, title of work, or both) following a direct quotation, consisting of at least one complete sentence, in footnotes or cited independently in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I felt an emotion...'. — Thirty Years, 1, 379. Use dash before citation following block/complete-sentence quotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid combining dash with other punctuation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash should not ordinarily be used in connection with any other point, except a period; do not combine dashes and commas around the same insertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not write constructs like 'DEAR SIR: — I have ...' or 'This, — I say it with regret, — was...' Use one form of bracketing punctuation, not both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses for enumeration markers run into text
rubrics_metrics.description: Place between parentheses figures or letters used to mark divisions in enumerations run into the text; if divisions are paragraphed, use single parenthesis with lower-case italic letters and period with figures/capitals according to scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the detailed schematic for multi-level lists (A., I., 1., a), (1), (a) etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses not ordinarily for parenthetical clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Parentheses should not ordinarily be used for parenthetical clauses unless confusion might arise from the use of less distinctive marks, or unless the content is wholly irrelevant to the main argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer dashes or commas for parenthetical matter that is relevant; parentheses reserved for aside or editorial notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brackets uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Brackets are used (1) to inclose an explanation or note, (2) to indicate an interpolation in a quotation, (3) to rectify a mistake, (4) to supply an omission, and (5) for parentheses within parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided for each numbered use; use brackets to make editorial clarifications or corrections within quoted material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bracketed 'continued' phrases formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases such as 'To be continued' at the end and 'Continued from ...' at the beginning of articles/chapters should be placed between brackets, centered, set in italics and in reduced type size according to reductions rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: [Continued from p. 320] ; [To be concluded]. Use italics and smaller type as indicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses to indicate omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipses are used to indicate the omission, from a quotation, of one or more words not essential to the idea being conveyed, and also to indicate illegible words, mutilations, and lacunae in quoted material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For an ellipsis at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence, four periods separated by a space (en-quad) should ordinarily be used except in very narrow measures; if preceding line ends in a point, do not include that in the four. For omitted paragraphs or lines insert a full line of periods separated by em- or 2-em quads as appropriate; periods should not extend beyond length of longest type-line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsis treated as part of citation
rubrics_metrics.description: An ellipsis should be treated as part of the citation; consequently should be enclosed in the quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include ellipsis within surrounding quotation marks to indicate omitted material from quoted text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation at line breaks and between compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is placed at the end of a line terminating with a syllable of a word, the remainder of which is carried to the next line, and between many compound words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply standard syllable division rules at line breaks; hyphenate compounds as described in subsequent rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate compound adjectives before a noun
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenate two or more words (except proper names forming a unity) combined into one adjective preceding a noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: well-known author, first-class investment, better-trained teachers, four-year-old boy. If components set in capitals or one component contains more than one word, use an en-dash instead of hyphen (FRANCO-PRUSSIAN WAR; New York–Chicago). Do not hyphenate adjectives or participles with adverbs ending in -ly, nor such combinations when following the noun or qualifying a predicate.
